items.title: Sudan Nashra: Burhan offers temporary immunity for internal dialogue participants | AU Peace, Security Council in Khartoum | Khartoum, Riyadh establish bilateral coordination council | Second-largest single group RSF defection arrive in Northern State
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . In an Armed Forces Day speech on August 14, Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan offered temporary immunity to participants in the intra-Sudanese dialogue his government is now rushing to launch, including a suspension of criminal proceedings against those facing charges while they take part. The move is largely aimed at clearing the legal obstacle facing leaders of the opposition Sumud coalition, the civilian coalition led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok that was formed on the back of a factional split in the the Civil Front for Democracy, a previous anti-war civilian front. The charges stem from that earlier coalition over what the military saw as proximity to the Rapid Support Forces. But the legal cases are only one obstacle. Civilian forces want the dialogue to follow a halt in fighting, input on how its preparatory arrangements are made and to know whether whatever comes out of the process will bind state institutions. The military is showing no sign of halting its campaign, while Burhan’s central role in building the dialogue and his apparent ambitions for it do little to settle questions about its independence. Moreover, Khartoum cannot entirely escape the regional and international tracks it is trying to outpace. An African Union diplomat told Mada Masr that any internal dialogue would ultimately need to connect with those tracks and gain acceptance from them. Khartoum may have seen an opening for some African cover. Just hours after Burhan’s speech, a delegation from the African Union’s Peace and Security Council arrived in Port Sudan before travelling to Khartoum for its first field visit to the capital since the outbreak of the war. Sudan has been trying to repair its relationship with the AU since 2021, when the bloc suspended its membership after the military and Rapid Support Forces jointly ousted the civilian wing of the government. Now, with state institutions back in Khartoum, a civilian government appointed last year and a domestic dialogue being hurried toward a September launch, authorities are looking for the AU’s renewed attention to translate into a role in the political process and the restoration of Sudan’s membership. But the visit is not quite the diplomatic endorsement Khartoum might want. Another AU diplomat told Mada Masr that the union is still assessing, speaking to multiple sides and gathering information. There is a lot the bloc needs to know, the diplomat said, and the AU is not prepared to give any political process a “blank check.” Monday was a busy day for what a Sudanese political source described as Khartoum’s effort to “rearrange its foreign relations during the war and beyond.” In Ankara, military Chief-of-Staff Yasser al-Atta held talks with his Turkish counterpart Selcuk Bayraktaroglu and Defense Minister Yasar Guler. Sudanese military sources said contacts between the two establishments have become more regular. The sources said Monday’s talks focused on the military’s needs at the current stage and the support it wants from Turkey after the war, from training and reconnaissance to rebuilding the armed forces’ capabilities and institutions. Turkey’s existing defense relationship with Sudan and its experience in areas where the military needs help make it one of the easier partnerships for Khartoum to deepen, one of the military sources said. On the same day, Burhan was in Riyadh signing the largest agreement in the history of Sudanese-Saudi relations, establishing a bilateral coordination council. A Sudanese diplomatic source said the council is intended to move the relationship “from managing scattered files to a single political and institutional mechanism.” The new mechanism is also intended to give the political relationship a more direct economic dimension, according to a former Sudanese diplomat. Political discussions with Riyadh can now be linked to projects in agriculture, energy, mining, infrastructure and trade. On the battlefield, both the military and the RSF are trying to take back territory following a series of gains by both sides in recent weeks. In Blue Nile, the military has stepped up air and artillery strikes on the RSF’s newly captured positions in Geisan and Kurmuk, while in North Kordofan, the RSF has launched drone attacks on towns recently captured by the military. The military received its second-largest batch of RSF defectors on Tuesday, with 318 fighters arriving in Northern State from North Darfur. A leadership figure in the Darfuri Mahamid tribe said some had coordinated their movements with security agencies beforehand, while others had made contact with previous defectors, including Al-Nour “Gubba” Adam, the former RSF commander in North Darfur and Mahamid tribal leader who defected earlier this year. *** Burhan offers temporary immunity for internal dialogue participants Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair and military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan gives a speech during the celebration of Armed Forces Day in Khartoum, August 14. Courtesy: Sudan News Agency In an Armed Forces Day speech on August 14 devoted largely to the intra-Sudanese dialogue his government has spent months championing, Burhan announced temporary immunity and legal and security guarantees for participants, along with a suspension of criminal proceedings against anyone facing charges during their involvement in the political process. The move is largely aimed at addressing the criminal cases against leaders of the opposition Sumud coalition based outside Sudan. The announcement comes after weeks of accelerated preparations in Khartoum for the domestic political track, which political sources told Mada Masr last week was being targeted for a September launch. The government is now working to settle the dialogue’s preparatory arrangements, the sources said, but those arrangements remain contested among the forces expected to take part. One of the political sources said last week that the government was preparing to clear the way for Sumud leaders facing charges to join the process. The measure may remove a legal barrier, but it does not resolve the larger dispute over how the dialogue should begin and who should control it. Many civilian forces, including Sumud, want any political process to follow a halt in fighting and a set of humanitarian and political guarantees. They are also seeking a role in determining the dialogue’s preparatory arrangements, rather than being asked to accept them once they are set. The cases hanging over Sumud’s leadership date back to a prosecution campaign that began in the first months of the war and widened as the government turned its attention to civilian political forces. In September 2023, the Public Prosecution announced arrest warrants for around 250 politicians, journalists and activists. The campaign expanded to include RSF commanders. And in April 2024, the Prosecution filed charges against 17 leaders of the Civil Front for Democracy, among them its leader and former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, on counts including inciting war against the state, incitement and complicity, as well as undermining the constitutional order, war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. Prosecutors later announced arrest warrants for 16 more politicians and moved to seek Interpol’s assistance. Many of those named in the charges now sit under a different banner. The Civil Front for Democracy splintered in February 2025, after members aligned with the RSF broke away to sign the founding charter of the RSF’s parallel government at its Nairobi conference. The remainder regrouped under Hamdok as Sumud, a coalition bringing together political parties, civil society organizations, unions, professional associations and resistance committees. Addressing the Armed Forces Day audience, Burhan said the state would provide participants with the guarantees they needed, but was careful to stress that the suspension of criminal proceedings was temporary and did not amount to an amnesty. The guarantees had already been on the table during consultations Burhan held with political forces in July, according to a political source close to Burhan informed of the TSC’s contacts. Their purpose, the source said, was to “remove the legal barrier to participation” while keeping the court cases formally in place, a distinction intended to prevent the invitation to dialogue from being read as a blanket political amnesty. But the guarantees need clear legal drafting — a defined timeframe and scope, a named authority empowered to order a suspension of proceedings and clarity over whether the protection would cover criminal charges alone or extend to arrest warrants and investigative proceedings, according to a legal source informed of the discussions. Sudanese judicial precedent shows that suspending criminal proceedings has followed defined legal frameworks, the source said, but the authority to order such suspensions and the limits of that authority have historically been contested. That leaves a gap between announcement and enforcement. The promise of temporary immunity still has to be translated into real decisions and executive procedures before it becomes a guarantee that participants can rely on, the source said. The most sensitive question will be whether charges or other legal restrictions can be used as leverage against participants while the dialogue is underway, as the state preserves its ability to resume proceedings once the guarantee expires, they added. Workable legal guarantees may clear one hurdle, but they leave a range of other objections unresolved. Shehab Ibrahim, a leader in Sumud, rejected the premise outright. He told Mada Masr that independence from the warring parties is a basic condition for the process to have any credibility. Holding a dialogue in territory controlled by either side, Ibrahim said, would entrench Sudan’s de facto division and reproduce the logic of the war rather than provide a path out of it. Another Sumud leader set a less sweeping condition, saying participation in a dialogue inside Sudan would require a halt in military escalation. Without that, the leader said, the process risks becoming little more than “a political arrangement for the existing authorities.” Legal guarantees are also not going to settle questions around the design of the process, according to a political source in the civilian forces following the consultations. Sumud and other civilian forces, the source said, want clarity on who will set the agenda, how the preparatory committee will be selected and whether the dialogue’s eventual outcomes will be binding on state institutions. Those concerns go to the central ambiguity in Khartoum’s model. The dialogue is meant to be independent, but is being built by the military-led state and alongside its efforts to reconstitute its institutions. The core bet within the TSC, according to a source close to the council and familiar with Burhan’s consultations, is to keep regionally and internationally sponsored tracks in a supporting role rather than as direct organizers. Burhan wants the dialogue to begin on a different footing from the political conferences held abroad over the past two years, the source explained, with Sudan’s existing institutions forming part of the environment in which the next political settlement is produced. In his speech, Burhan sought to distance his government from criticism that the process is state-curated, saying a “national group” of Sudanese had taken the initiative in proposing it “of their own accord.” He called it “an independent national mechanism,” with the state providing only “logistical support” and the necessary guarantees. But that description sits uneasily with how the process has been built so far, as Burhan himself has spent weeks leading consultations with political forces, tribal leaders and national figures, building the political backing for the dialogue and shaping the arrangements around its launch. A political source in the civilian forces close to those consultations said the mechanism will also face practical limits on its independence if its organizers depend on state institutions for funding, protection and facilitation, even as Khartoum seeks to present it as separate from executive and military authority. The question of independence also runs up against what an informed political source previously told Mada Masr Burhan envisions the dialogue to be: a vehicle for rebuilding state institutions. Burhan’s speech earlier this week placed the two agendas next to each other. He said forces that backed the state and its institutions during the war would take part in completing those institutions, including the long stalled legislative council, whose formation is currently under consultation. A political source in government-allied civilian forces familiar with these arrangements said reconstituting the legislative council is one of the tracks Khartoum wants to advance alongside the dialogue. An informed former Sudanese diplomat sees clear political significance in the pairing. Khartoum, in their view, is trying to build a political framework for the coming phase before it can be pressured into a final settlement of the war. “The dialogue here isn’t happening in an institutional vacuum,” the diplomat said, but at a moment when the authorities are working to entrench their institutions and redefine the basis of political participation. The military-led government’s political track, naturally, does not amount to a truce track. Burhan’s speech offered no indication that his government is prepared to suspend military operations. That puts the government at odds with several of the political forces being considered for the process, which have made a halt in fighting and a conducive humanitarian and political environment conditions for their participation. Burhan said the military would continue what he called “completing the cleansing of the country from the terrorist militia,” and repeated the military establishment’s longstanding condition that the RSF must withdraw from the cities before any peace process could begin. A military source close to the leadership said there is no contradiction, in its view, between continuing military operations and pursuing political movement. Military pressure, the source said, is intended to create the conditions for a political settlement built “on foundations that preserve the unity of Sudan and end with dismantling the RSF.” Meanwhile, the Quintet — the African Union, United Nations, Arab League, European Union and Intergovernmental Authority on Development — is preparing to resume its consultations on a political process, after its meetings in Addis Ababa in late July failed to bring the political forces into a joint discussion or produce agreement on the proposed preparatory arrangements. That failure is what created an opening for Khartoum to push ahead with its own domestic track, a political source informed of the process told Mada Masr last week. Burhan’s moves through July and August suggest that the government is trying to establish its process before the regional and international consultations arrive at a conclusion of their own. An AU diplomatic source said the two efforts would eventually have to connect. Any successful internal dialogue, they said, would need acceptance from the regional and international tracks, even if Khartoum organizes it domestically. According to the source, the question is ultimately less about where the dialogue takes place, but whether it can produce a workable political consensus, and whether that consensus can be linked to an end to the war and to humanitarian and security arrangements. *** AU Peace and Security Council delegation arrives in Khartoum TSC Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and a delegation from the African Union’s Peace and Security Council meet in Khartoum, August 16. Courtesy: The TSC Just hours after Burhan’s speech, a delegation from the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, headed by Mohamed Khaled, the council’s rotating chair for August, arrived in Port Sudan on Saturday and travelled to Khartoum the following day. It was the council’s first visit to the capital since the outbreak of the war. Like many regional and international organizations, the AU withdrew its staff and closed its offices there when fighting began. More than three years later, Khartoum is under military control, and the state has spent the past year re-establishing the capital as its seat of power in a campaign that has outpaced its capacity. The return of state institutions has begun to draw regional bodies back toward the capital, with some showing interest in reopening offices and restoring direct contact. Khartoum sees the visit as an opening to repair relations with the continental body and draw African support toward the political process led from the capital. Tasis, the RSF-led government, has objected to the visit, concerned that it could help establish Khartoum as the state’s sole political center. But AU and Sudanese diplomats said the visit should not be interpreted as an endorsement of the government or its political process, but is part of a process of listening and assessment. Khartoum had been waiting for a field visit that would allow the council to assess developments inside the capital following the military’s recapture of Khartoum and the return of state institutions, a Sudanese diplomatic official said. They described the visit as “a first step toward rebuilding the relationship between Khartoum and African institutions.” That relationship has been strained since 2021, when the AU suspended Sudan’s membership after the military and RSF jointly removed the civilian wing of the transitional government instituted following the ouster of former President Omar al-Bashir, saying it “strongly condemns the seizure of power” and branding it “unconstitutional.” It said the suspension would remain in place “until the effective restoration of the civilian-led transitional authority.” The authorities have sought to return to the bloc since the military retook Khartoum last year and the state began appointing a civilian government and reinstating transitional institutions. Khartoum’s efforts to reverse the suspension have yet to produce a change in Sudan’s status. Sources in the continental body previously told Mada Masr that a ceasefire agreement and the launch of a credible political process remain key prerequisites for lifting it. The visit, in the view of an AU diplomat informed of the delegation’s program, allows the council to “engage with the Sudanese reality from within,” rather than relying on briefings from missions and mediators. During its stay, the delegation met with Burhan, Prime Minister Kamel Idris, government officials and political forces, discussing “the political, security, and socioeconomic and humanitarian situation,” the council stated . The government saw the delegation’s arrival as evidence that Khartoum was once again drawing the AU’s attention. For Khartoum, it was “a signal that Sudan is back at the top of the continental institution’s agenda,” according to a Sudanese political official informed of contacts with the AU. The authorities want that attention to lead to concrete steps: an end to Sudan’s suspension and a more direct African role in supporting the internal dialogue. But the council’s return to Khartoum does not amount to an endorsement of the political process there. The AU “wants to know who is running the process, who is guaranteeing its inclusiveness and whether its outcome will actually lead to constitutional arrangements,” a second AU diplomatic source said. Those questions will shape the council’s assessment in the coming period, they added. With the war still underway and political and military forces remaining outside Khartoum, the source said, the AU is not prepared to give the process a “blank check.” A government-aligned political source involved in the initial consultations over the state-led dialogue said the delegation’s arrival had nevertheless raised hopes that the initiative could gain regional recognition. But the source similarly said the AU would need to ensure that the process was not simply a “reshuffling of the political house in areas under government control.” Khartoum, meanwhile, wants to use the opening to make the case that a political solution can begin from within Sudan while continuing to frame the RSF as a rebel force, the source added. Idris made that position explicit in his meeting with the African delegation. According to a statement from the Cabinet, he laid down “red lines” for any political process, foremost among them a rejection of any equivalence between the armed forces and the RSF. He called on the AU to support the government’s efforts to have the RSF designated a terrorist organization. The position puts Khartoum at odds with the central premise of the international effort around Sudan — that ending the war will require bringing the country’s competing political and military forces into a negotiated settlement. The AU has pursued that objective both independently and through the Quintet, in efforts to bring Sudanese parties together and lay the groundwork for a new transitional arrangement. But the AU’s support for an inclusive political process does not mean accepting rival centers of government. Khaled affirmed during the meeting the council’s rejection of attempts to create parallel governments that could undermine Sudan’s unity and sovereignty. “The only path to achieving lasting peace in Sudan is through dialogue, national reconciliation and reaching a comprehensive political settlement that meets the aspirations of the Sudanese people,” he said. The visit drew opposition from the RSF-led government. On Tuesday, Tasis Prime Minister Mohamed al-Taaishy sent a letter to the Peace and Security Council objecting to the delegation’s trip to Khartoum and its meetings with the authorities there. He called on the council to deal with Sudanese parties even-handedly. A political source close to Tasis told Mada Masr that the concern was that the visit could become a step toward treating the Khartoum government as the state’s sole center of authority, particularly after government institutions returned to the capital. “The problem for Tasis is not the AU visiting Sudan, but Khartoum becoming the only address the council listens to,” the source said. Tasis, they added, wants African engagement to extend beyond the capital, including to areas controlled by other parties. But a Sudanese diplomatic source and the AU diplomat informed of the delegation’s program said the meetings in Khartoum do not amount to a final AU position on Sudan’s broader political arrangements. According to the AU diplomat, the council is hearing from multiple parties while operating within its previous decisions on Sudan. The Khartoum visit is “part of a process of listening and assessment,” the diplomat said, and the AU’s eventual position on any political process will be based on the outcome of its contacts with the various sides. *** Military chief-of-staff in Ankara Military Chief-of-Staff Yasser al-Atta, his Turkish counterpart Selcuk Bayraktaroglu and Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Guler meet in Ankara, August 17. Courtesy: Sudan News Agency Military Chief-of-Staff Yasser al-Atta arrived in Ankara on Monday on an official visit at the invitation of his Turkish counterpart Selcuk Bayraktaroglu and Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Guler. According to a Sudanese diplomatic source informed of relations between Khartoum and Ankara, the visit focused on “developing military cooperation between the two countries and opening files related to training, capacity building and technical cooperation.” The source told Mada Masr that the visit comes as contacts between the two military institutions have become more regular. “The presence of the military chief of staff in Ankara, and his reception by the Turkish defense minister, reflects the level the military relationship between the two countries has reached,” the source said. Sudan is now seeking to broaden its defense ties with countries that have shown a willingness to work with Sudanese state institutions, they added. According to a Sudanese military source informed of the visit, the talks are tied to the military’s needs, created by more than three years of war. These range from training, communications, reconnaissance and operational management. The military is also looking to rehabilitate a number of its institutions and facilities, the source added. Turkey’s experience in these areas makes it a useful partner as the Sudanese military reorganizes its capabilities, a second military source said. The source did not say whether the discussions covered particular systems or equipment. Ankara and Khartoum had already expanded cooperation into defense and military industries in the years before the war, the first military source said, describing the current effort as the “reactivation and expansion of existing channels in line with the needs created by the war.” That history gives Ankara an advantage over countries with which Sudan would have to build military ties from scratch. “Turkey is one of the countries with which a partnership can be developed more quickly,” a third Sudanese military source said. The Ankara diplomacy is part of a wider attempt by Khartoum to “broaden its network of foreign relations,” a Sudanese political source informed of the country’s foreign affairs told Mada Masr. The government is pursuing several relationships at once, including with Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the AU and neighboring countries. “Khartoum wants its relationship with Turkey to be part of a broader arrangement of its foreign relations during the war and beyond,” they added. Atta’s visit, however, carries a significance beyond the usual political diplomacy, a second Sudanese diplomatic source said. By sending the military chief of staff to Ankara, the military establishment itself is taking part in the process of reshaping Sudan’s external relationships, they added. The military is also beginning to look beyond the immediate demands of the war and toward what comes after it, when, the source said, Sudan will need to “rebuild the capabilities of the armed forces and its institutions.” The military relationship also benefits from the broader ties spanning political, humanitarian and economic areas already linking Sudan and Turkey, according to a former Sudanese diplomat who served at the Sudanese embassy in Ankara and a Turkish diplomat at the Turkish embassy in Sudan. A former Sudanese diplomat said the timing is also significant because it coincides with Khartoum’s moves on the internal dialogue and international efforts to mediate the war. “The government wants to enter any upcoming political arrangements with a more balanced network of foreign relations,” they said. For Ankara, the Turkish diplomat said, Sudan is “a strategically important country in the Red Sea and Horn of Africa region.” Maintaining communication with Sudanese official institutions is part of Turkey’s policy toward Sudan, the source said. Turkey significantly upgraded its involvement in Sudan following the fall of Fasher in October 2025, expanding its support for the Sudanese military. An Egyptian official told Mada Masr at the time that Ankara is pursuing a strategy in Sudan that is similar to the one it adopted in Libya in 2020 against the Libyan National Army — an intervention that effectively froze the war along distinct eastern and western spheres of influence, and ultimately cemented Ankara’s influence in Tripoli. *** Khartoum, Riyadh establish bilateral coordination council Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin Salem and his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud sign the agreement establishing the Sudanese-Saudi Coordination Council, in Riyadh, August 17. Courtesy: Saudi Foreign Affairs Ministry Sudan and Saudi Arabia inked the largest agreement in the history of their bilateral relations in Riyadh on Monday. Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin Salem and his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan al-Saud signed the agreement establishing the Sudanese-Saudi Coordination Council, nearly ten months after Saudi Arabia formally set the process in motion. The council is meant to bring the relationship under a comprehensive institutional umbrella, with a mandate covering ten areas including politics, security, economic affairs, investment and trade, according to a source at Sudan’s Foreign Ministry. The ministry said it would also facilitate joint projects and programs. A Sudanese diplomatic source informed of Khartoum-Riyadh relations described its purpose as moving ties “from managing scattered files to a single political and institutional mechanism,” bringing economic, political and investment matters together rather than leaving them spread across ministries and different bilateral contacts. The agreement follows a process that began on October 21, 2025, when the Saudi Council of Ministers authorized the foreign minister or his deputy to negotiate and sign an agreement with Sudan on establishing the council. Its creation has since moved through Saudi Arabia’s formal government channels. For Khartoum, the council comes as it seeks to put its war-long political relationship with Riyadh on more durable footing, the diplomatic source said. A former Sudanese diplomat informed of the relations said Khartoum sees Saudi Arabia as one of the few capitals able to combine political weight with economic capacity, giving Riyadh a particular place among the capitals Sudan is seeking to cultivate as political and economic partners. For Riyadh, the relationship with Sudan is tied to the kingdom’s interests in Red Sea security, humanitarian files and economic and investment interests. The council gives those interests a more formal structure through which they can be pursued, the first diplomatic source said. A Sudanese source informed of the economic file said the council would allow Khartoum and Riyadh to connect political negotiations directly to economic projects, with agricultural investment, energy, mining, infrastructure and trade among Sudan’s priority areas. The council’s practical value will hinge on the ability of its committees to translate agreements into concrete timelines and projects, a Sudanese official involved in earlier talks with the Saudi side told Mada Masr. Sudan needs a follow-up mechanism capable of cutting through slow government procedures and connecting agreements to implementation. But implementation will also depend on conditions beyond the council’s internal mechanisms. A Sudanese official in charge of economic files told Mada Masr that the war has made investment increasingly contingent on security, stability and legal guarantees, particularly in sectors requiring long-term capital. *** Military downs 3 RSF drones in North Kordofan, pushes west Military troops announce shooting down an RSF drone over Gabra al-Sheikh in North Kordofan, August 15. Courtesy: @AbedaMoham6183 on X Three RSF strategic drones were shot down over North Kordofan this week as the military pushed westward from positions it captured last month, sweeping areas around Gabra al-Sheikh, according to two military sources who spoke to Mada Masr. The first of the three drones, an FH-95, was shot down over Gabra al-Sheikh on Saturday, the military said. Two more drones of the same type were brought down on Monday, one over Gerigikh and the other over Bara. A military source told Mada Masr that the military’s surveillance systems and drones detected and destroyed the RSF drones before they could reach their targets. All three towns fell to the military in late July, when a two-day ground offensive seized one of the RSF’s most important logistics hubs in North Kordofan. The RSF has since been trying to recover the territory, mounting attacks on the newly captured positions. To stem the attacks, the military advanced on Saturday from Gabra al-Sheikh westward and cleared the areas of Kogmor and Abu Hadid, which had been used as a launching point for the RSF’s attacks on Gabra al-Sheikh last week. The sweep reached the outskirts of Mazroub, around 150 km southwest of Gabra al-Sheikh, a second military source said. The military’s advance has also extended into West Kordofan. On Wednesday, it regained control of Mamsouka in Sunut locality, along the road connecting Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, to Nuhud in West Kordofan, according to the source. The military has also targeted the supply network supporting RSF positions farther west. Military aircraft struck RSF supply lines in Abu Zabad on Monday, destroying seven fuel tankers, as well as supply warehouses in Khawi, the Dar Hamar emergency room in West Kordofan stated . The escalation in fighting has seen the RSF move personnel out of the area this week. The second military source said the RSF gathered captured military personnel and abducted civilians held in North Kordofan on Monday and transported them toward North Darfur in cargo trucks. A day later, according to the Dar Hamar emergency room , the RSF evacuated wounded fighters from northern localities in neighboring West Kordofan, transporting them to Nyala in South Darfur in 40 cargo vehicles. *** Military hits RSF positions after Blue Nile’s Kurmuk, Geisan losses The military has stepped up air and artillery strikes across the Blue Nile front following last week’s RSF advances into the towns of Kurmuk and Geisan, while its forces in the Kurmuk locality have repelled ground and drone attacks, according to a field source in the military-allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), led by Malik Agar. On Tuesday, following intelligence surveillance, the military destroyed a launch platform for suicide drones and killed its crew before the platform could be used in an attack on the Baraka garrison near Kurmuk, the source told Mada Masr. The source said the garrison had also repelled a ground assault the previous day by the RSF and its ally, the SPLM-N (Hilu) faction led by Joseph Tuka, inflicting heavy casualties and destroying military equipment. Air and artillery strikes have meanwhile intensified along the Geisan front, particularly around Khor Dahab and Khartoum Bileil. The strikes have killed and wounded fighters and destroyed vehicles and other military equipment, the source said. Some wounded RSF and SPLM fighters have been transferred to a hospital in the Ethiopian city of Asosa in recent days, they added. The military’s strikes have prompted competing claims over the condition of a key bridge in the area. RSF-supporting media platforms had reported that military artillery struck the bridge over Khor Tammat, which connects Amoura and Bakory in the Geisan locality. They said the strike was aimed at blocking an RSF advance toward Damazin, the Blue Nile capital. The Geisan locality administration denied the reports, saying the Tamat bridge remained intact and undamaged. The administration accused the RSF of circulating the claim to conceal its battlefield losses and create fear that could discourage displaced residents from returning. The bridge is an important crossing for the surrounding communities, particularly during the rainy season, when damage to the route could significantly restrict movement. The latest fighting follows a major RSF and SPLM advance on the Blue Nile front last week. The two forces captured Geisan and, two days later, retook Kurmuk, both near the Ethiopian border, across which the attacks were launched, according to three military sources who spoke to Mada Masr at the time. The offensive has brought the two sides back into a fight over the state’s most strategically important border positions, only weeks after the military recaptured Kurmuk. The key cross-border gateway had fallen to the RSF and SPLM-N in March after the allies moved into Blue Nile from Ethiopia, opening a route for supplies and military support to reach their forces. Despite the losses, the military retains several garrisons in Kurmuk and Geisan localities, including Baraka, Keili and Sali in Kurmuk and Bakory in Geisan, according to a former military officer who spoke to Mada Masr. The officer said military forces remained deployed in the area as part of a plan to wear down the RSF before launching offensives to take back the two towns. *** Joint force says it secured North Kordofan’s Ambro after taking Kreiker The joint force of military-allied armed movements took control of Kreiker in North Darfur, a strategic node between the towns of Tawila, Kutum and Ambro. The force’s spokesperson said to the press that the operation secured Ambro. A joint force field source told Mada Masr that the assault on Kreiker was one of a series of rapid operations targeting RSF concentrations and disrupting its supply lines, rather than an effort to establish a permanent presence in the area. The force is likely to withdraw from Kreiker after the operation, the source said. The assault inflicted losses on the RSF, including the death of a prominent commander in the area who was related to RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo, the source added. The operation comes after a week of fighting and shifting control around Ambro. The joint force briefly entered the town last week before withdrawing following clashes with the RSF. The RSF captured Ambro, along the Chadian border, on June 23 as part of an offensive that brought the group deeper into the Zaghawa tribal territory, where the military retains its last positions in Darfur following the fall of Fasher last year. *** Second-largest single group RSF defection arrive in Northern State Former RSF commander Musa “Khamseen” Ahmed speaks to the press after his defection, August 19. Courtesy: @sport6780 on X A force of 318 fighters and 50 combat vehicles arrived in the Northern State city of Dabba on Tuesday, in the second-largest single group to defect from the paramilitary force in recent weeks. The fighters arrived with their weapons and equipment, according to a military source and a tribal leader who spoke to Mada Masr. The military source said preparations to receive the force in Northern State had been underway for several days with the support of military intelligence. Another RSF commander also defected and arrived in Northern State on Wednesday, the source said, adding that authorities were making arrangements before releasing further details. Anwar Ahmed Khater, head of the Mahamid tribal coordination committee, told Mada Masr that Tuesday’s group had come from Tawisha, Um Kadada and surrounding areas in North Darfur. The fighters were familiar with the desert routes leading toward military-held areas, he said, allowing them to avoid RSF ambushes and checkpoints on their way to Dabba. Khater said some in the group had coordinated their movements in advance with security agencies, while others had established contact with previous defectors, including Al-Nour “Gubba” Adam, the former RSF commander in North Darfur and Mahamid tribal leader who defected earlier this year. Musa “Khamseen” Ahmed, the commander of the force that arrived in Dabba, told the press that the decision to join the military was prompted by what he described as a lack of institutional work within the RSF and disappointment with the Tasis project. At a reception for the force, Mohamed Saleh Younes, the commander of the military’s Border Guards, said the doors remain open to anyone wishing to return to the military’s ranks. Khater said defections could affect the RSF’s capabilities in ways that direct military confrontations may not, given the group’s reliance on tribal mobilization and recruitment. He said the conduct of the war had contributed to the defections and that some tribal groups were increasingly reluctant to continue fighting alongside or supporting the RSF. He added that the RSF has come to rely more heavily on foreign fighters from Colombia, South Sudan, Chad and elsewhere. The latest arrival follows the defection in late July of 280 RSF fighters who reached Omdurman in 30 combat vehicles to join the military, according to a senior military officer who spoke to Mada Masr at the time. Those fighters had previously served under Gubba in Darfur. *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . The post Sudan Nashra: Burhan offers temporary immunity for internal dialogue participants | AU Peace, Security Council in Khartoum | Khartoum, Riyadh establish bilateral coordination council | Second-largest single group RSF defection arrive in Northern State first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: It’s Low-Calorie and Packed With Protein. Is It Healthy?
items.description: Ice cream is one of life’s simplest and most enduring culinary pleasures. The first published recipe, which dates back to the 17th century, combined milk, water, sugar, and candied citron or pumpkin. By the early 20th century, companies were regularly adding stabilizers to their ice creams to prevent them from getting freezer burn and artificial dyes to give them appealing hues. But the core essence of ice cream—sweetened, frozen dairy—remained largely unchanged into the 21st century. Even Halo Top, the diet ice cream that surpassed Ben & Jerry’s as the nation’s best-selling in 2017, simply subbed in skim milk and artificial sweeteners to keep the calories down. Then came David. The protein-bar company has turned its attention to “frozen dessert,” which is, of course, more commonly known as ice cream, though the company can’t legally call their product that. Instead of being made with cream and milk, it comprises a “protein system,” a “structure system,” a “fat system,” and a “flavor system,” each of which is composed of ultra-processed ingredients such as whey protein isolate and “modified plant fat.” The only whole natural ingredients on the vanilla flavor’s label are water, salt, and vanilla bean. And yet, the treat’s basic nutritional stats are impressive: A pint has just 210 calories, less than 1 gram of sugar, and 30 grams of protein. Unlike diet ice creams of the past, it is rich and creamy. When the product launched on David’s website in June, it sold out in 28 minutes. (The company declined to tell me how many units it sold.) David’s ice cream is perhaps the most outwardly refined of a whole category of frozen desserts that are being deliberately packed with protein. These protein-ice-cream companies and others processing their way to a palatable nutrition label are making a bet on what Americans truly want from food. We (and our government) might have grown more skeptical than ever of industrially produced foods, but we also expect quite a lot from every morsel we consume. When I recently spoke with Brendan Niemira, the chief science and technology officer of the Institute of Food Technologists, he spent nearly two minutes listing qualities that Americans now desire: that food be tasty and safe, sure, but also low-calorie, high-protein, probiotic, full of omega-3 fatty acids, and so on. Last month, PepsiCo launched a powdered oatmeal drink, with 15 grams of protein, that dissolves in cold milk or water. It also makes a prebiotic version of Pepsi that contains 3 grams of fiber and does not taste like Metamucil. Kraft Heinz recently introduced a mac and cheese with 17 grams of protein and 6 grams of fiber, thanks largely to a “proprietary protein-and fiber-enriched pasta.” Nestlé offers a 45-calorie “pre-meal hunger support nutritional drink” that is composed almost entirely of industrially processed ingredients and that the company says helps people feel full sooner. At the Institute of Food Technologists’ annual conference earlier this summer, I feasted on “better-for-you BBQ pizza,” the crust of which was fortified with wheat-protein isolate, and watermelon-lime “satiety soda” that was spiked with corn fiber. I even ate frozen yogurt that starred a “network of cell-signaling peptides from the fava bean” and was supposed to help me recover from workouts. On paper, Americans are generally wary of such products: In a June 2025 survey, more than 60 percent of respondents said they believe that ultra-processed foods are addictive. And some experts worry that the ingredients such products depend on—emulsifiers, preservatives, and sugar substitutes—are somehow messing with our metabolism, such that the impressive macros of these products don’t provide the full picture of their healthfulness. (The FDA approves the safety of such additives, but that review process historically has focused on toxicity and, say, cancer risk, not metabolic effects.) Many believe that the manipulation of ingredients causes our bodies to react in unforeseen ways to the food we eat—that a manufactured “protein system” might not be beneficial in the way that, say, lentils’ protein system is. Or they note the simple fact that many UPFs—even those that may be high-protein, probiotic, or high-omega-3—still contain a lot of fat, sugar, and salt, which are clearly bad for us. Take PepsiCo’s SunChips Fiber, which launched in March. A 7-ounce bag of the chips—seven servings, according to the company, but honestly not that enormous of a snack—has 21 grams of fiber, most of what the FDA recommends an adult eat in a day. But it also has 910 calories. Even if these fiber-filled SunChips had fewer calories, UPF critics would point to the way they’re made—using an industrial process called extrusion, which essentially pulverizes grains into easily digestible morsels—as a potential danger. (Some researchers suspect that extruded grains spike insulin more than their unprocessed counterparts.) The problem is that the science around which processing steps and industrial ingredients might actually be harmful is still in its infancy. And it will struggle to catch up with the food industry’s innovation. Major food companies are regularly creating new processes for spiking foods with nutrients without making them taste like health foods. Nestlé’s “hunger support” drink, for example, uses something the company calls “whey protein microgels,” which help prevent the drink from getting too thick in the manufacturing process. David’s frozen dessert is so low-calorie and yet so indulgent because of that “modified plant fat,” a chemical called esterified propoxylated glycerol that is not absorbed by the digestive tract and was cleared for use in food by the FDA in 2015. (An earlier nondigestible fat, olestra, infamously flopped after people began reporting that it was causing them “anal leakage” in the ’90s; safety studies of EPG indicate that such leakage could occur with very high doses.) Scientists might be convinced that extrusion can make an otherwise healthy product like whole grains metabolically harmful. But what about “supercritical fluid extrusion” that—according to Frito-Lay, which patented the technology—uses less heat and thus can “deliver high levels of fruits or vegetables” in a still-crispy snack? Until experts can articulate precisely why ultra-processed health foods are a problem, we’ll all be stuck in limbo. Companies will continue offering ever more processed and refined health foods, made with shiny new ingredients and methods; meanwhile, some experts will continue warning Americans that we should not eat them, without being able to back those warnings up with data on the latest foods. Every time a new processed health food hits the shelves, anyone who visits a grocery store will have to guess whether this one will be truly healthy. In the face of some uncertainty, at least some Americans are, so far, turning to products such as David’s: The company sold $131 million worth of its protein bars in their first year on the market. Most Americans don’t actually need more protein in their diet, and certainly they could get it without spending about $9 on a pint of David. “This so-called ice cream looks to me a boondoggle for all concerned, save those selling it at, no doubt, extremely high profit margins,” David Katz, the founding director of the Yale-Griffin Prevention Research Center, told me via email. But David’s CEO, Peter Rahal, told me his detractors are luddites. He argued that people need more protein than the daily recommended amount to “thrive,” and that having the option of a new diet ice cream on the shelf shouldn’t be controversial. “You want the full-fat, full-cream, full-sugar thing that has this amazing heritage, go for it. But if you want something that’s really close to taste and texture, that’s more advanced and more sophisticated, it should be there for you,” he said. (David’s product is so expensive, Rahal said, because of the cost of whey protein.) Clearly, some Americans see the world like Rahal does. When the craving for ice cream hits, a pint under 300 calories has its own appeal—even if it’s not ice cream at all.

items.title: Modernisation de l’offre de soins à Thiès : Plus de 690 millions de FCFA investis dans l’acquisition d’équipements médicaux
items.description: Dans le cadre de la poursuite de la politique de modernisation de l’offre de soins dans la région de Thiès, le ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique a investi plus de 690 millions de FCFA dans l’acquisition d’équipements médicaux destinés aux hôpitaux et aux structures de soins de santé primaires. Le ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique poursuit sa politique de modernisation de l’offre de soins dans la région de Thiès. Ainsi, à l’approche du Maouloud, la tutelle a procédé, le 20 août 2026, à une évaluation du dispositif sanitaire et des investissements réalisés dans la région. A lire aussi : Kaolack : 1 387 agents mobilisés pour la couverture sanitaire du Gamou ! « Plus de 690 millions de FCFA ont été investis dans l’acquisition d’équipements médicaux destinés aux hôpitaux et aux structures de soins de santé primaires. Les infrastructures en cours de réalisation représentent plus de 12 milliards de FCFA, hors nouvel hôpital Seydi El Hadji Malick Sy de Tivaouane, dont l’investissement s’élève à 46 milliards de FCFA », informe le ministère à travers une note publiée vendredi. La même source indique qu’à une semaine de l’événement, les activités de prévention avaient déjà permis de visiter 3 791 concessions, de sensibiliser 18 955 personnes et de traiter 1 585 sites. La surveillance de la qualité de l’eau, le contrôle de la salubrité, la désinfection, la désinsectisation et l’encadrement des opérations de nettoiement ont également été renforcés. Plus de 3 000 agents de santé seront mobilisés dans la région pour le Maouloud 2026 Sur ce, un dispositif sera mis en place pour garantir aux fidèles une couverture sanitaire accessible, réactive et sécurisée durant le Maouloud. Ainsi, plus de 3 000 agents de santé seront mobilisés pour assurer gratuitement la prise en charge des pèlerins. Le dispositif comprend notamment : 45 postes médicaux avancés et 14 postes médicaux de référence ; 60 ambulances, dont 6 ambulances de réanimation ; 24 points de couverture des principaux axes routiers ; plus de 35 véhicules de liaison et de supervision. Il est aussi prévu deux cliniques mobiles, une clinique odontologique et plusieurs laboratoires et près de 100 millions de FCFA en médicaments et produits de santé pour la région de Thiès. Mariama DIEME

items.title: Sénégal-Pays-Bas : la coopération policière au centre d’une rencontre à Dakar
items.description: Le directeur général de la Police nationale, l’Inspecteur général de Police Mame Seydou Ndour, a reçu, jeudi 20 août 2026, une délégation de la Police nationale du Royaume des Pays-Bas, en présence de ses collaborateurs et de représentants des directions techniques spécialisées. Facilitée par l’Office des Nations unies contre la drogue et le crime (ONUDC), cette rencontre s’inscrit dans le cadre du renforcement de la coopération bilatérale entre les deux pays dans le domaine de la sécurité. Les échanges ont notamment porté sur les priorités nationales en matière de sécurité intérieure, à travers une présentation des orientations du ministère de l’Intérieur et de la Sécurité publique. Les deux parties ont également abordé la lutte contre la criminalité organisée et le trafic de stupéfiants, ainsi que les moyens de renforcer la coopération opérationnelle entre les services de police. Cette coopération devrait notamment s’appuyer sur le partage d’expériences, le renforcement des capacités et l’appui à la formation professionnelle. L’Inspecteur général de Police Mame Seydou Ndour a salué cette initiative, estimant qu’elle contribue à consolider les synergies internationales en vue d’une lutte plus efficace contre la criminalité transnationale organisée. La rencontre s’est achevée après des échanges consacrés au renforcement des mécanismes de coopération entre les services de police sénégalais et néerlandais.

items.title: PTI slams govt for ‘flouting’ SC order, opp says it will approach SC over contempt
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The PTI on Friday accused the government of committing contempt of court by “flouting” the Supreme Court’s order to shift incarcerated party founder Imran Khan to Shifa International Hospital, and announced that it would approach the apex court on Saturday. On Tuesday, the SC had directed the government to move Imran to Shifa International Hospital, a private facility. All eyes were on the hospital with a heavy police presence stationed on Thursday night. However, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar revealed on Friday that Imran was instead taken to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims). It is worth mentioning that the SC had ordered that Imran’s medical reports or information concerning his health should not be used for political purposes. On Friday, Imran’s sister Uzma Khan, who was present for his medical examination, addressed a press conference in Islamabad alongside his personal physician, Dr Faisal Sultan. She said they had received a phone call on Thursday to reach Adiala jail, where Imran is incarcerated. “So we reached the Adiala jail at around 8-8:30pm,” she added. Uzma said they were then taken to a deputy superintendent of police’s room, whom she identified as Sibtain. “Later, Sibtain sahib asked Dr Sultan to go outside the room with him and me to stay in the room. Then, after around 10 to 15 minutes, a female assistant sub-inspector took me to a car.” She added that all this while, police did not answer any of her queries, including those about Dr Sultan. Uzma said she was then taken to Pims. “I asked them why you have brought me here; the SC has instructed for (Imran’s) treatment at Shifa International Hospital. At that, they told me we were there for a follow-up regarding Imran’s eye.” Imran has been taken to Pims for treatment multiple times after his eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — came to light in late January. Recounting her visit to Pims on Thursday night, Uzma said, “There was darkness all around.” She said she was taken to an office as a man used the torch from his mobile phone to light the way. She said she assumed the office belonged to the head of a department at Pims. “We sat there for a while, and then they took me upstairs. When I went upstairs, Imran was sitting there. He too was a little surprised. He then stood up, he was in shock. He told the doctors who were with him that she is my sister and we were meeting after 10 months,” she recalled. Uzma said she told him he was there for a checkup and would later be taken to Shifa International Hospital, adding that she also enquired about Dr Sultan at Pims but received no response. She said they were then taken back to an office, where an examination of Imran’s eye was conducted. “There were two to three doctors there, but I was not familiar with any of them. They introduced me to Dr Arif, but I did not know any of the others,” she said. She said they were then taken to an office where an examination of Imran’s eye was conducted. “They asked, ‘Khan sahib , which eye drops do you use?’ “I said if the drops they had prescribed were not mentioned in their notes. None of them knew,” she added. One of the doctors said Imran needed to immediately undergo a test as his blood vessel had to be checked, she recalled, adding that she told the doctors they would be going to Shifa International Hospital for an examination and checkup. Uzma said they were again shifted to another place after that, where the doctors said Imran had to be administered an injection. They also did other tests and said the eye condition and haemorrhage situation had improved, she said. Then, a doctor came and checked Imran’s blood pressure, which was 120/80 or 70, she said. “He (Imran) asked me what was happening, and I told him he would be taken to Shifa International Hospital for complete examination and, if required, any treatment. He was happy with that,” she recalled. All this while, Uzma said, Imran kept telling her just one thing: that he had been subjected to “cruelty”. “He said they were torturing them. He said a doctor who had visited him had concluded that his health deteriorated due to not having any human contact. “He said he was not provided any reading material or television for the past 10 months,” she said. Uzma added that Imran also said when he would complain about his health to prison doctors, “no one would listen or care”. She further quoted him as telling her that a doctor who examined him on August 10 said that he had severe anxiety due to “mental torture in solitary confinement”, and that anxiety caused high blood pressure. Uzma said that, complaining of his health condition, Imran said Egyptian president Mohamed Morsi “was killed the same way, by giving him stress and keeping him in solitary confinement”. “He also said that Bushra Bibi was also being kept in solitary confinement […] He kept saying that they were subjecting him to cruelty,” Uzma said, adding that Imran told her that he was given newspapers and television for two days, after which these facilities were taken back. She also rejected reports that Imran was not happy about being taken to Shifa International Hospital. Continuing her account, Uzma said they were taken to the Adiala jail instead of Shifa International Hospital from Pims. “When I disembarked the car I was in, I saw Dr Sultan getting off another car,” she said, adding that Imran’s message for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sohail Afridi was to expedite and intensify his movement. Speaking after her, Dr Sultan said he was taken to Shifa International Hospital from the Adiala jail while Uzma was taken to Pims. “There were security arrangements there, and I was asked to wait at the hospital. We kept waiting for around two to two and a half hours. I kept asking and they kept on saying that he (Imran) was arriving. I think they, too, were not completely aware of what the plan exactly was. “Around 4:15-30pm, they told me that it seemed he (Imran) may not be able to come, and he probably had returned, and that I too should return,” he said. Dr Sultan said he saw Uzma disembarking from another car upon reaching the Adiala jail, and then the two came to know that they were taken to separate hospitals. Replying to a question, Uzma said Imran was not aware of the situation outside as he did not have access to newspapers and television. To a query about Imran’s health, she said he was “fit”, his blood pressure was normal and vision had improved. “Just a small haemorrhage is left,” she added. KP CM Afridi also spoke at the press conference, expressing regret over the government and administration’s conduct on Thursday. “A decision by three judges of the Supreme Court was thrown in the dustbin,” he said, terming the act contempt of court. “Judges across Pakistan now have to decide whether to get their decisions implemented or shut courts,” he remarked. As Uzma conveyed Imran’s message to him, he said he would be expediting his movement for Imran’s release. Moreover, he said, the PTI would file a contempt plea over Thursday night’s episode. The KP CM also rejected claims that any PTI workers had gathered outside Shifa International Hospital on Thursday night. Opposition to approach SC on Saturday The opposition’s joint parliamentary party on Friday said the government had committed contempt of court by failing to implement the SC’s order to shift incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan to Shifa International Hospital, and announced that it would approach the apex court on Saturday. According to a statement released by opposition alliance Tehreek Tahafuz Ayeen-i-Pakistan (TTAP), the opposition’s joint parliamentary party held a meeting at Parliament House, chaired by National Assembly Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai and attended by Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and other leaders. The meeting discussed the country’s overall political situation, the health of the PTI founder, the implementation of the apex court’s orders, parliamentary affairs and the opposition’s future political and public strategy, the statement said. During the meeting, serious concern was expressed over the non-implementation of the SC’s orders to shift Imran to Shifa International Hospital, and it was decided to adopt a “constitutional and legal course of action”, it added. “The joint parliamentary party members stated that by failing to execute the Supreme Court’s verdict, the government has committed contempt of court,” the statement said, adding, “Consequently, it was decided to approach the Supreme Court tomorrow.” The meeting participants expressed “deep concern” over the health of Imran. The members “categorically stated that no compromise would be accepted regarding his health and medical treatment, noting that the government had staged a drama concerning his well-being,” the statement claimed. Regarding the September 27 long march, the meeting announced its decision to uphold the PTI’s plan for a full-scale protest on the announced date, it stated. “Detailed consultations were held regarding the September 27 protest and long march, with a decision to invite all opposition parties to participate.” According to the statement, the meeting agreed to intensify the public contact campaign across the country, including Punjab, and make political activities more organised and effective. “The joint parliamentary party expressed its firm resolve to continue a united struggle for the protection of the Constitution, democracy, the rule of law and parliamentary principles. “It was decided that the opposition parties would make all future key political and parliamentary decisions through mutual consultation, unity and solidarity,” the statement said. The TTAP statement added that the meeting participants fully endorsed the establishment of the grand opposition alliance, agreeing to make the coalition more “active, organised and effective”. It also welcomed the inclusion of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman and other opposition parties in the grand opposition alliance, stating that a broader alliance would further strengthen and amplify the opposition’s voice, both in parliament and among the public. “Detailed consultations were held on the opposition alliance’s future political, parliamentary and public strategy, with an agreement to further accelerate mutual coordination and consultation in this regard,” the statement concluded. ‘Theatrics and misleading conduct’ Separately, PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram also criticised the government for what he described as an “attempt to conceal its non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s order”. Referring to Tarar’s X posts, he said they had once again “exposed the government’s familiar pattern of theatrics and misleading conduct”. “The Supreme Court’s order has not been implemented and only a superficial exercise had been carried out to mislead the court and the nation,” Akram said in a statement. He added that “declaring the PTI founder medically fit after a few hours of what appears to have been a merely symbolic exercise and then shifting him back to the Adiala jail before dawn raises serious questions”. Moreover, “blaming PTI workers with false allegations to conceal the violation of a court order is not a new tactic but an old pattern of government theatrics and deception”, he said, adding that PTI workers had not gathered at Shifa International Hospital, nor had they created any security concerns. “There are no media reports of any security situation,” he stated. “Conducting a secret transfer in the middle of the night and then blaming PTI workers for compromising security exposes the contradictions and falsehoods in the government’s own narrative.” He demanded that the government make Imran’s complete medical reports public and implement the Supreme Court’s order in letter and spirit. “Imran Khan’s health is not a matter of political propaganda; it is a fundamental human right. Instead of engaging in political theatrics, the government must ensure full compliance with the directions of the SC,” he asserted. “Things are not as simple as Attaullah Tarar is attempting to portray them,” he continued, adding that mere statements and symbolic measures were not sufficient. “The government must ensure transparency in the matter of Imran Khan’s health and provide him with the required medical facilities and an independent medical examination, as directed by the court.”

Le groupe italien de défense Leonardo ouvre une filiale en Ukraine et veut y tester son nouveau système de défense aérienne «Michelangelo Dome»
items.description: Le groupe italien de defense Leonardo a enregistre une nouvelle filiale en Ukraine le 20 mai 2026, avec son siege a Kiev. Baptisee Leonardo Ukraine, elle appartient entierement au groupe par l'intermediaire de Leonardo International. Selon le quotidien economique et financier italien MF-Milano Finanza du 19 août 2026, il ne s'agit pas d'un simple bureau de representation, mais d'une entite juridique distincte integree au groupe. Cette implantation accroît la presence directe de Leonardo dans le secteur militaro-industriel ukrainien. La societe doit mener des activites de recherche et de developpement et intervenir dans plusieurs secteurs a usage militaire, parmi lesquels les equipements de communication, les instruments de mesure et de navigation, les materiels specialises, les logiciels ainsi que les systemes electroniques et optiques. Les drones constituent egalement l'un des axes de cette presence. Le directeur general de Leonardo, Lorenzo Mariani, a justifie cette orientation par l'experience acquise en Ukraine pendant le conflit. « Nous devons cooperer avec l'Ukraine, qui a acquis une experience pendant le conflit », a-t-il declare, en indiquant que les appareils sans pilote feraient partie des principaux domaines concernes. L'Ukraine envisagee comme terrain d'essai L'un des principaux objectifs concerne le futur systeme de defense aerienne Michelangelo Dome. Selon MF-Milano Finanza , Leonardo envisage de tester en Ukraine certains de ses composants dans des conditions reelles, en utilisant ainsi le contexte du conflit pour poursuivre le developpement de technologies militaires. Michelangelo Dome doit relier plusieurs moyens de detection, de commandement et d'interception au sein d'une meme architecture. Le projet comprend notamment un module MC5 dote d'elements d'intelligence artificielle charges de traiter les donnees recues et de participer a la gestion des menaces aeriennes. L'installation d'une structure permanente a Kiev permet ainsi a Leonardo d'aller au-dela de la seule livraison de materiels. Le groupe dispose desormais d'un cadre juridique local pour mener des recherches et developper des projets militaires tout en envisageant des essais directement sur le territoire ukrainien. Drones, intelligence artificielle et industrie de defense Leonardo prevoit egalement de travailler avec Brave1, la plateforme ukrainienne consacree aux technologies de defense. Selon les informations rapportees par MF-Milano Finanza , elle rassemble environ 2 500 entreprises et plus de 5 000 solutions technologiques. Des donnees associees a l'entreprise americaine Palantir sont notamment utilisees pour l'entraînement d'algorithmes militaires reposant sur l'intelligence artificielle. Le groupe italien poursuit en parallele ses projets dans le secteur des drones. Il a deja conclu un accord avec le constructeur turc Baykar pour creer une entreprise commune dediee aux appareils militaires sans pilote. Cette implantation survient sur fond de hausse des depenses militaires europeennes et d'implication croissante des industriels occidentaux dans le secteur de la defense ukrainienne. Moscou denonce regulierement les livraisons d'armes, le financement militaire de Kiev et l'elargissement de la presence des groupes de defense occidentaux en Ukraine, estimant que cette politique contribue a prolonger les hostilites. Avec Leonardo Ukraine, un nouveau groupe europeen dispose ainsi d'une presence directe dans le secteur militaro-technologique ukrainien. Le pays pourrait desormais etre utilise non seulement pour des projets lies aux drones et a l'intelligence artificielle, mais egalement comme terrain d'essai en conditions de conflit pour certains composants du futur systeme de defense aerienne Michelangelo Dome.

items.title: Somalie : 1,9 million d’enfants menacés par la faim et la malnutrition
items.description: La crise alimentaire et nutritionnelle s'aggrave en Somalie, ou pres de 1,9 million d'enfants devraient etre touches par la malnutrition cette annee, a alerte le 21 août l'Unicef. Selon l'agence des Nations Unies pour l'enfance, le nombre d'enfants admis dans les structures de sante pour des cas de malnutrition aigue severe accompagnee de complications a augmente de 32 %. La situation est aggravee par les reductions importantes de l'aide humanitaire. Depuis le debut de l'annee, 205 centres de sante et de nutrition ont deja ferme, tandis que jusqu'a 618 structures pourraient etre contraintes de fermer a l'echelle nationale, a indique James Elder, porte-parole de l'Unicef, lors d'une visioconference. « Moins de structures signifie des trajets plus longs pour les meres et leurs bebes ; des voyages plus longs signifiant un traitement plus tardif ; un traitement plus tardif signifie des maladies plus graves et un risque accumule de deces evitables », at-il averti. Pres d'un demi-million d'enfants menaces par une malnutrition aigue Parmi les 1,9 million d'enfants exposes a la malnutrition cette annee, pres de 500 000 devraient souffrir de malnutrition severe, consideree comme la forme la plus dangereuse de la maladie. Le financement destine a lutter contre la malnutrition aigue dans certaines regions de Somalie a chute de plus de 80 % cette annee, selon Medecins sans frontieres. Les etats-Unis ont notamment interrompu une partie de leurs financements, tandis que plusieurs autres pays occidentaux ont egalement reduit leur aide. Pour l'Unicef, ces coupes interviennent au pire moment. La Somalie est confrontee simultanement a une crise climatique croissante, avec une secheresse severe dans certaines regions du nord, ainsi qu'aux conflits et aux deplacements de populations. La hausse des coûts du carburant et des engrais vient encore alourdir les difficultes auxquelles sont confrontees les populations. « C'est le mauvais moment pour se retirer », a souligne James Elder, appelant au maintien et au renforcement de l'aide humanitaire. L'agence onusienne craint que la fermeture progressive des structures sanitaires n'eloigne davantage les enfants des soins dont ils ont besoin, malgre ainsi les risques de complications et de deces lies a une malnutrition pourtant evitable et traitable lorsqu'elle est prise en charge a temps.

items.title: Nando: durcissement des contrôles des prix des produits de grande consommation
items.description: ​(Réo, le 21 août 2026). La Direction Régionale de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat (DRICA) de Nando durcit le contrôle des produits de grande consommation sur les marchés de Réo. Sucre, riz, huiles alimentaires, savon, ciment, œufs, gaz et autres produits réglementés sont passés au crible. ​Les contrôleurs ont relevé plusieurs infractions, dont la pratique de prix illicites, le stockage clandestin et la vente de produits périmés ou prohibés. Une quantité importante de produits impropres à la consommation a été retirée du marché.​Les contrevenants s’exposent aux sanctions prévues par la réglementation. La DRICA appelle les consommateurs à signaler tout acte de fraude ou de spéculation sur les prix. Numéros verts : ​80 00 11 84 ​80 00 11 85 ​80 00 11 86 ​DCRP/MICA DRICA-Nando L’article Nando: durcissement des contrôles des prix des produits de grande consommation est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Ceuta: démantèlement d'un réseau de passeurs soupçonné de faire payer jusqu'à 9000 euros par traversée
items.description: La police espagnole vient de démanteler un réseau de passeurs entre l’enclave espagnole de Ceuta, au nord du Maroc, et la péninsule. Au moins cinq personnes ont été arrêtées ces derniers jours, à Ceuta et dans la ville andalouse de La Línea de la Concepción, soupçonnées d’avoir fait payer jusqu’à 9 000 euros pour la traversée du détroit de Gibraltar. Les migrants font partie des 72 000 personnes entrées illégalement le 31 juillet dans l’enclave depuis le Maroc.
